notes.heading: Four ways to describe redox
points: Oxidation: gain of oxygen, loss of hydrogen, loss of electrons, or increase in oxidation state. Reduction is the opposite in each case.
OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss of electrons, Reduction Is Gain of electrons.
Oxidation state treats shared electrons as fully given to the more electronegative atom. Write the sign first: +1, not 1+.
Oxidizing agent is reduced and takes electrons; reducing agent is oxidized. Name whole species (HBr), not single atoms (H).
Disproportionation: one substance is oxidized and reduced in the same reaction, e.g. KClO3 forming KClO4 and KCl.

notes.heading: Half-equations and balancing
points: A half-equation shows only oxidation or only reduction, with electrons on the right for oxidation and the left for reduction.
Electrons per half-equation equal the size of the oxidation state change; multiply so electrons lost equal electrons gained, then cancel.
In acid, balance O with H2O and then H with H+. In neutral or basic solution, use OH− for O and H2O for H.
Finish by checking total charge is equal on both sides, e.g. 6Fe2+ + Cr2O7 2− + 14H+ → 6Fe3+ + 2Cr3+ + 7H2O.

notes.heading: Ease of oxidation and reduction
points: Halogens act as oxidizing agents; ease of reduction increases up the group, so F2 is strongest, I2 weakest.
A more reactive halogen oxidizes the halide ions of a less reactive one: Cl2 + 2Br− → 2Cl− + Br2.
Group 1 metals are reducing agents; ease of oxidation increases going down the group.
If a metal reacts with another metal's ion solution, it is more easily oxidized and a stronger reducing agent. Order metals by these results.

notes.heading: Acids with reactive metals
points: Reactive metals (Mg, Zn, Fe) react with dilute strong acids to give a salt plus hydrogen gas.
Metal is oxidized (reducing agent); H+ is reduced (oxidizing agent): 2H+ + 2e− → H2.
Metals below hydrogen in the reactivity series, such as copper and silver, do not react with dilute acids.
Hydrogen is detected by a lit splint giving a pop.

notes.heading: Anode and cathode
points: Oxidation occurs at the anode; reduction at the cathode (RED CAT).
Electrons flow through the external wire from the oxidation site to the reduction site.
Without a salt bridge, charge builds up (polarization) and the reaction stops.

notes.heading: Primary (voltaic) cells
points: A primary cell turns energy from a spontaneous redox reaction into electrical energy; its reaction is not reversible.
Parts: two half-cells (metal in its ion solution), wire to voltmeter, and a salt bridge completing the circuit.
Salt bridge ions flow to balance charge: cations toward the cathode half-cell, anions toward the anode half-cell.
Cell diagram: anode on left, cathode on right, salt bridge as ||, e.g. Zn(s) | Zn2+(aq) || Cu2+(aq) | Cu(s).
Zn anode gets thinner and Cu cathode gets coated; blue Cu2+ colour fades.

notes.heading: Secondary cells and fuel cells
points: Secondary cells have reversible redox reactions: an applied electric current recharges them. Charging reverses the discharge reactions.
Compared with primary cells, they meet higher current demands but self-discharge faster.
Lead–acid discharge: Pb anode oxidized, PbO2 cathode reduced, overall Pb + PbO2 + 2H2SO4 → 2PbSO4 + 2H2O.
Lithium-ion: Li oxidized at the anode on discharge; electrolyte must be non-aqueous because lithium reacts with water.
Fuel cells need a continuous fuel and oxygen supply, are not rechargeable, and run indefinitely; hydrogen ones make no greenhouse gases but use costly catalysts and pure hydrogen.

notes.heading: Electrolytic cells
points: An electrolytic cell turns electrical energy into chemical energy by driving non-spontaneous reactions (electrolysis).
Parts: electrolyte (molten or aqueous ionic compound), two electrodes, and a DC power source.
Cathode is connected to the negative terminal: cations are reduced there. Anions are oxidized at the anode.
Molten NaCl: cathode Na+ + e− → Na; anode 2Cl− → Cl2 + 2e−.

notes.heading: Oxidation of organic compounds
points: Secondary alcohol is oxidized to a ketone; primary alcohol to an aldehyde and then a carboxylic acid.
Reflux with excess oxidizing agent and acid gives the carboxylic acid; vapours condense back into the flask.
Distillation with alcohol in excess removes the aldehyde as it forms, preventing further oxidation.
Tertiary alcohols are not oxidized this way because the carbon with OH has no hydrogen to remove.

notes.heading: Reduction of organic compounds
points: Ketone is reduced to a secondary alcohol; carboxylic acid is reduced via an aldehyde to a primary alcohol.
Reduction adds hydrogen atoms to the carbonyl group, written [H] for the reducing agent.
The aldehyde intermediate from a carboxylic acid usually cannot be isolated.
LiAlH4 reduces all of these; NaBH4 reduces only aldehydes and ketones, though specific agents are not assessed.

notes.heading: Reducing unsaturated compounds
points: Adding hydrogen to a C=C or C≡C bond is reduction and lowers the degree of unsaturation.
Alkyne to alkene needs a deactivated palladium catalyst.
Alkene to alkane needs a Ni or Pt catalyst; excess hydrogen takes an alkyne straight to alkane.

notes.heading: Standard hydrogen electrode
points: The SHE is H+(aq) + e− ⇌ ½H2(g), with E⦵ = 0 V by convention, using an inert platinum electrode.
More negative E⦵ means easier oxidation and a stronger reducing agent; more positive means easier reduction.
Standard conditions: 298 K, 100 kPa, and 1.0 mol dm−3 for all aqueous species.
Standard reduction potentials are in section 19 of the data booklet.

notes.heading: Standard cell potential
points: E⦵cell = E⦵(cathode) − E⦵(anode), which equals E⦵(reduced species) − E⦵(oxidized species).
A spontaneous reaction has positive E⦵cell. Reduction is at the more positive electrode.
Do not multiply E⦵ when doubling a half-equation to balance electrons.
Example: Fe/Cu cell gives +0.34 − (−0.45) = 0.79 V.

notes.heading: Gibbs energy and cell potential
points: ΔG⦵ = −nFE⦵cell, where n is the electrons transferred in the balanced equation.
F = 9.65×10^4 C mol−1; the equation and F are in the data booklet.
Positive E⦵cell gives negative ΔG⦵, so the reaction is spontaneous.
Units: J mol−1; divide by 1000 for kJ mol−1. Example: n = 2, 0.76 V gives −147 kJ mol−1.

notes.heading: Electrolysis of aqueous solutions
points: Water competes with ions: reduction H2O + e− → ½H2 + OH− (−0.83 V); oxidation H2O → ½O2 + 2H+ + 2e−.
At cathode, if the cation's E⦵ is more negative than −0.83 V, water is reduced and hydrogen forms.
Concentrated NaCl(aq): H2 at cathode, Cl2 at anode (high Cl− beats water); dilute gives mixed O2 and Cl2; very dilute gives O2.
CuSO4(aq), inert electrodes: Cu at cathode; sulfate cannot be oxidized (S already +6), so O2 forms at anode.

notes.heading: Electroplating
points: Electroplating coats an object, made the cathode, with a thin layer of metal by electrolysis.
The anode is the plating metal; it oxidizes to cations that travel through the solution and are reduced onto the cathode.
Copper plating: anode Cu → Cu2+ + 2e−; cathode Cu2+ + 2e− → Cu. Electrolyte concentration stays constant.
With impure copper as anode, pure copper plates onto the cathode, which purifies it.

definitions.definition: Loss of electrons, or an increase in oxidation state. Also gain of oxygen or loss of hydrogen.
definitions.trap: Giving only electron loss when the question asks for oxidation numbers.

definitions.definition: Gain of electrons, or a decrease in oxidation state. Also loss of oxygen or gain of hydrogen.
definitions.trap: Mixing it up with oxidation; use OIL RIG.

definitions.definition: A species that accepts electrons from another species, causing its oxidation, and is itself reduced.
definitions.trap: Naming the atom rather than the whole compound, e.g. H instead of HBr.

definitions.definition: A species that donates electrons to another species, causing its reduction, and is itself oxidized.
definitions.trap: Swapping it with oxidizing agent; the reducing agent is the one oxidized.

definitions.definition: The charge an atom would have in a compound if all bonds were treated as ionic, with shared electrons given to the more electronegative atom.
definitions.trap: Writing the sign after the number (1+) or treating it as a real charge.

definitions.definition: An equation showing only the oxidation or only the reduction process, with the electrons lost or gained.
definitions.trap: Leaving electrons out or putting them on the wrong side.

definitions.definition: A reaction in which the same substance is simultaneously oxidized and reduced.
The electrode in an electrochemical cell where oxidation occurs.
definitions.trap: Calling the anode positive in every cell; it is negative in a voltaic cell but positive in an electrolytic cell.

definitions.definition: The electrode in an electrochemical cell where reduction occurs.
definitions.trap: Remember RED CAT: reduction at the cathode in both cell types.

definitions.definition: A tube or strip containing an ionic salt solution that connects the half-cells, letting ions flow to balance charge and complete the circuit.
definitions.trap: Saying electrons flow through the salt bridge; electrons use the wire.

definitions.definition: An electrochemical cell that converts energy from a spontaneous redox reaction into electrical energy; its reaction is not reversible.
definitions.trap: Confusing it with a secondary cell, which can be recharged.

definitions.definition: A cell whose redox reactions can be reversed by applying electrical energy, so it can be recharged.
An electrochemical cell that converts electrical energy to chemical energy by driving non-spontaneous redox reactions.
definitions.trap: Mixing up its electrode charges with a voltaic cell.

definitions.definition: The use of an external DC electrical source to bring about non-spontaneous chemical change in an electrolyte.
A half-cell of H+(aq) at 1.0 mol dm−3 and H2 gas at standard pressure on inert platinum, assigned E⦵ = 0 V.
definitions.trap: Omitting that it is the reference and that conditions are standard.

definitions.definition: The potential of a half-cell, under standard conditions with 1.0 mol dm−3 solutions, measured relative to the standard hydrogen electrode.
definitions.trap: Leaving out the standard hydrogen electrode or the standard conditions, which examiners often mark as incomplete.

definitions.definition: The voltage of a cell under standard conditions, found as E⦵(cathode) − E⦵(anode); positive for a spontaneous reaction.
definitions.trap: Multiplying E⦵ by the coefficient used to balance electrons.

definitions.definition: Coating an object with a thin layer of metal by electrolysis, with the object as the cathode.
definitions.trap: Putting the object at the anode.

definitions.definition: An electrochemical cell that converts the chemical energy of a continuously supplied fuel and oxygen directly into electrical energy.
definitions.trap: Calling it rechargeable; it is not, it just keeps being fed.

definitions.definition: Heating a reaction mixture with a condenser fitted so vapours cool and return to the flask, giving complete oxidation.
definitions.trap: Mixing it up with distillation, which removes the product.
